--- Comment #7 from Peter Dalgaard (<mailto:pd.mes@cbs.dk|pd.mes@cbs.dk>) ---
Yes (to Suharto), conversion algorithms is the culprit

If we avoid going via large integers, and go by the definition, we get

> a <- 0; m <- 1 ; for (i in 1:16){m <- m/10; a <- a + 9*m}
> sprintf("%a",a)
[1] "0x1.fffffffffffffp-1"
> 1-a
[1] 1.110223e-16

or, just doing the last digit this way:

> .999999999999999 + 9*1e-16 
[1] 1
> sprintf("%a", .999999999999999 + 9*1e-16 )
[1] "0x1.fffffffffffffp-1"
> .999999999999999 + 9*1e-16 -1
[1] -1.110223e-16

but curiously

> 999999999999999*1e-15 + 9*1e-16 -1
[1] 0
> sprintf("%a", 999999999999999*1e-15 + 9*1e-16)
[1] "0x1p+0"

However, negative powers of 10 come with their own representation issues:

> 1e-16 - 1e-8*1e-8
[1] -1.232595e-32

or even 

> 0.01 - 0.1 * 0.1
[1] -1.734723e-18

so perhaps better look at stuff like

> sprintf("%a",999999999999999/1e15 + 9/1e16)
[1] "0x1.fffffffffffffp-1"

*[Bug 19095] New: `loadNamespace()` performance issue with many `importFrom()`*
<https://bugs.r-project.org/show_bug.cgi?id=19095>

            Bug ID: 19095
           Summary: `loadNamespace()` performance issue with many
                    `importFrom()`
           Product: R
           Version: R 4.6.x
          Hardware: Other
                OS: Other
            Status: UNCONFIRMED
          Severity: enhancement
          Priority: P5
         Component: Low-level
          Assignee: <mailto:R-core@R-project.org|R-core@R-project.org>
          Reporter: <mailto:lionel.hry@gmail.com|lionel.hry@gmail.com>

Created attachment 3744
  --> <https://bugs.r-project.org/attachment.cgi?id=3744&action=edit>
Benchmark

A single `importFrom(pkg, sym1, sym2, ...)` scales much better during namespace
loading than consecutive `importFrom(pkg, sym1); importFrom(pkg, sym2); ...`
directives (which is what roxygen2 generates). The attached patches make the
consecutive style load as fast as the grouped style.

Current R (baseline):

```
N=10     many       2.0 ms
N=10     one        2.0 ms
N=100    many      10.0 ms
N=100    one        2.0 ms
N=1000   many     131.5 ms
N=1000   one        6.0 ms
N=10000  many    5756.0 ms
N=10000  one       48.0 ms
```

With the first patch which avoids computing the names of a big exports
environment for each import-from iteration:

```
N=10     many       2.0 ms
N=10     one        2.0 ms
N=100    many       9.0 ms
N=100    one        2.0 ms
N=1000   many      96.0 ms
N=1000   one        5.0 ms
N=10000  many    2434.5 ms
N=10000  one       46.0 ms
```

With the second patch that merges adjacent import-from directives for the same
package at install time:

```
N=10     many       2.0 ms
N=10     one        2.0 ms
N=100    many       2.0 ms
N=100    one        2.0 ms
N=1000   many       5.0 ms
N=1000   one        5.0 ms
N=10000  many      45.0 ms
N=10000  one       46.0 ms
```

While N=10k is extreme, a few 100s or even a 1000 imported symbols might occur
with large packages.

- roxygen2 generates individual `importFrom()` expressions.

- We're considering expanding bulk imports to explicit `importFrom()`
directives to pin the set of imported symbols and prevent package updates from
creating user-visible conflicts at load-time.

The install-time merge implemented here benefits every package, hand-written or
roxygen2-generated, with no author action needed. Separately we plan to have
roxygen2 emit merged `importFrom()`s so older R versions benefit too.

__builtin overflow checks in arithmetic.c

Following up from r-devel:
<https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-devel/2026-June/084615.html>

The initial motivation here is that `R_integer_times`, as currently
implemented, relies on Undefined Behavior (UB):

```
// stylized from arithmetic.c
int z = x * y;
if ((double)x * (double)y == z && z != NA_INTEGER)
  return z;
```

I.e., _after_ running the multiplication in `int`, we check if wraparound
happened _in `double`_ (into which `int` embeds faithfully). The comment in the
code acknowledges this is UB.

My initial proposal was to use `int64_t` instead, but Brian points out it is
not universally available and indeed it's basically not used elsewhere in the R
sources. The widely available `int_fast64_t` seems much more appropriate here
than `int_least64_t`.

Luke also mentions `__builtin_mul_overflow` [1][2], which are recent enough
(e.g. 2015) to necessitate some `configure` checks to activate, but which _are_
supported by `gcc` and `clang`.

On r-devel, I mentioned a quick benchmark in support of moving away from
`double` -- now I've made that more formal by running the benchmark on GitHub
Actions in the R mirror [3] by adding in `reg-tests-2.R` a snippet:

```
x <- y <- rep(10000L, 5e7)
print(system.time(for(i in 1:100) x * y))
```

And extracting the timings from 4 different proposals [4][5][6][7]. 

Here is the benchmark timings table (unit: seconds) compiled from the logs:

| Flavor | baseline | int64_t | int_fast64_t | \_\_builtin\_mul\_overflow |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Linux (clang, debian:stable, arm)** | 14.084 | 12.915 | 12.815* | 13.521 |
| **Linux (clang, debian:stable, intel)** | 15.528 | 10.573 | 10.694 | 10.379*
|
| **Linux (clang, debian:testing, arm)** | 14.400 | 12.896 | 12.757* | 13.799 |
| **Linux (clang, debian:testing, intel)** | 15.487 | 10.776 | 10.612* | 10.639
|
| **Linux (gcc, debian:stable, arm)** | 14.940 | 12.588 | 12.518* | 14.285 |
| **Linux (gcc, debian:stable, intel)** | 13.983 | 10.046 | 9.318* | 9.441 |
| **Linux (gcc, debian:testing, arm)** | 14.731 | 12.707* | 12.870 | 14.386 |
| **Linux (gcc, debian:testing, intel)** | 14.753 | 11.719 | 10.903 | 8.704* |
| **MacOS (macOS-26)** | 8.977 | 10.001 | 8.855* | 11.006 |
| **MacOS (macOS-26-intel)** | 22.831 | 21.492 | 21.802 | 20.030* |
| **Windows (aarch64)** | 12.250 | 11.050 | 10.980* | 11.940 |
| **Windows (x86_64)** | 14.990 | 6.350* | 12.250 | 11.310 |

Note that these timings all have a fair amount of overhead from R -- I'm trying
to make it a bit more realistic to show how the end user will perceive the
change. This is of course far from comprehensive. Another way to view this is
comparing the assembly output of the two approaches (`double` vs.
`int_fast64_t`). Consider this minimized script:

In the generated assembly (`gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel compare.c -o compare.s`, and
similarly for `clang`), I see:

```
times_double:
.LFB0:
        .cfi_startproc
        mov     r8, rdx
        cmp     edi, -2147483648
        je      .L2
        cmp     esi, -2147483648
        sete    cl
        je      .L2
        pxor    xmm0, xmm0
        pxor    xmm1, xmm1
        mov     eax, edi
        cvtsi2sd        xmm1, esi
        cvtsi2sd        xmm0, edi
        mulsd   xmm0, xmm1
        imul    eax, esi
        pxor    xmm1, xmm1
        cvtsi2sd        xmm1, eax
        ucomisd xmm0, xmm1
        setnp   dl
        cmovne  edx, ecx
        test    dl, dl
        je      .L5
        cmp     eax, -2147483648
        je      .L5
        ret
        .p2align 4,,10
        .p2align 3
```

Compared to:

```
times_fast64:
.LFB1:
        .cfi_startproc
        mov     rcx, rdx
        cmp     edi, -2147483648
        je      .L14
        cmp     esi, -2147483648
        je      .L14
        movsx   rdi, edi
        movsx   rsi, esi
        mov     edx, 4294967294
        imul    rdi, rsi
        lea     rax, 2147483647[rdi]
        cmp     rdx, rax
        jb      .L15
        mov     eax, edi
        ret
        .p2align 4,,10
        .p2align 3
```

`cvtsi2sd`, `mulsd`, and `ucomisd` are all relatively expensive compared to
`movsx`, `imul`, and `cmp`.

So to me, this is really about whether we should use `int_fast64_t` or
`__builtin_mul_overflow`. The appeal of the latter is that it is _designed_
explicitly for what we're trying to do. The code is also quite clean.

Lastly, while this started from improving integer _multiplication_ in this
file, we might as well address the checks for overflow in _subtraction and
addition_ while we're at it. The principle is the same -- we can refactor to
either (1) explicitly embed in a 64-bit type, probably `int64_t` or (2) use
`__builtin_{add,sub}_overflow`. It's not formalized yet, but a quick benchmark
shows a similar conclusion -- we can do way better than the current
implementation with either approach.

I think all of the approaches are pretty straightforward; I'm attaching a PoC
patch of the `__builtin_{add,sub,mul}_overflow`.
